chapter_theme: The opening of Pattinathar's Arutpulambal, a lament addressed to the Lord of Kannivanam: the poet does not know his origin or his end, is maddened by impurity and deeds, and finds every desire in him (for land, gold, women, children, kingship, learning, siddhis, mantras, food, the senses, lust and anger, fear and ego) refusing to leave in the first person, while women's bodies announce that they will ruin him. The chapter ends with the beginning of a long litany: are the days spent as grass, stone, animal, god, demon, king, mother, wife and child not enough?
structure_note: The whole work is in short two-line units with the refrain கன்னிவனநாதா, which the text prints as a separate line every four units (438, 442, 446, 449, 454, 458). The units fall into runs by their closing word: எனக்கு verbs (434 to 437), ஆசை ... என்குதே, where each desire speaks for itself (438 to 447), எண்ணுதே (447 to 449), the body's parts threatening the poet (450 to 452), a direct plea (453), and the போதாதோ litany of births that continues into chapter 29 (454 to 458). The refrain's கன்னிவனம் is taken by tradition as a name of Kanchipuram, and 453 makes the Lord addressed the father of Kandan, so Siva.

434.reading: I do not know the root, I do not know the end that ends; the suffering met in the world walks on, seeking.
434.nuance: மூலம் and முடிவு set the frame: the poet's ignorance is of where he came from and where it ends, the question Sivavakkiyar presses at 989 and 1006. நாட நடக்குதடா can be read as the suffering walking on in search, or as the poet going on in search of it.

435.reading: By the impurity that is ignorance, understanding and the rest were lost; by the fruit of deeds that do not part, I was seized by madness.
435.nuance: அறியாமையாம் மலம் identifies the first impurity with ignorance, as Saiva Siddhanta does with ஆணவம். The verse gives two causes in order, impurity and deeds, and madness (பித்து) as the result; the whole lament that follows is spoken as a madman's.

436.reading: The four beginning with the body I took as myself and was bewildered; I was caught in the net of the powers beginning with mantra.
436.nuance: தனுவாதி நான்கு is traditionally the four products of maya, body, organs, worlds and enjoyments (தனு, கரணம், புவனம், போகம்). மனுவாதி சத்தி is less clear: மனு may be mantra, so the powers that start with mantra (perhaps the six adhvas), or it may be the human and other orders. Either way the verse says the self was lost in what maya made.

437.reading: In the forest called great maya I wander; the elements of all the worlds are troubled as if of themselves.
437.nuance: மாமாயை is the mahamaya of Siddhanta, the pure maya above the impure. தாது may be the bodily humours or the elements, and தாமாய் (of themselves, as if they were I) is hard to place; the line may mean that the poet takes all the world's stuff for himself, continuing 436.

438.reading: The desire for land has had me eaten by land; the desire for gold and the desire for women say 'I will not go'.
438.nuance: The three desires, மண், பொன், பெண், are the standard Tamil triad (மூவாசை). மண்ணுண்டு போட்டது is a pun: land eaten the lover of land, as the earth eats the buried. From here to 447 each desire is made to speak in the first person, என்குதே, so the poet's will is shown as not his own.

439.reading: The desire for children and kin says 'I will not forget'; the desire that is kingship of the quarters says 'I will not end'.
439.nuance: திக்கரசு, rule of the directions, is the ambition of universal kingship; set beside children and kin it ranges desire from the hearth to the world.

440.reading: The desire to learn the arts says 'I will not leave off'; the desire to learn siddhis says 'I will not be broken'.
440.nuance: The siddhis, the Siddhars' own goal, are named here as one more craving beside learning; the verse treats the wish for powers as a bond, not a path.

441.reading: The desire for mantras says 'I will not forget'; the desire for beauty says 'I will not renounce'.
441.nuance: சுந்தரம் may be the beauty of others or the poet's own adornment; the verse does not say which. Mantras follow siddhis (440) as a second item of religious craving.

442.reading: The desire for the kind that binds says 'I will not come loose'; the desire in trade and thrift says 'I will not be broken'.
442.nuance: கட்டுவர்க்கம், the binding class, may be the household and its ties or the whole category of bonds. செட்டு is thrift or trading, which fits the tradition that Pattinathar was a merchant before his renunciation; the verse itself only names the desire.

443.reading: The washed clothes I change says 'I will not forget'; the rice pit, too, says 'I will not yet be filled'.
443.nuance: சோற்றுக்குழி, the pit for rice, is the belly, and தூரேன் (I will not be filled in) is said of a pit. Fine laundered clothes and food are the body's own desires, after the mind's in 438 to 442.

444.reading: The five senses say 'we will not subside'; the mind's fretting says 'I will not settle'.
444.nuance: தேறேன் (I will not clear) is said of water and of the mind: the agitation itself refuses to clear. The senses and the mind join the list of speakers, so the poet's whole apparatus talks back.

445.reading: Lust and anger say 'I will not pass'; and every day the thought comes that we ourselves are king.
445.nuance: நாமே அரசு is the ego's claim of sovereignty, said daily (நாடோறும்). The pairing காமக் குரோதம் is the Sanskrit kama-krodha, taken as one compound.

446.reading: Fear and egoism say 'we will not subside'; the ... too says 'I will not come loose'.
446.nuance: கைச்சு மின்னுமான் is obscure; கைச்சு may be bitterness (கசப்பு) or a word for the hand's grasp, and மின்னும் may be இன்னும் (still). The first line is clear: fear and ahamkara join the list.

447.reading: The thought takes the body, a bubble on water, for permanent; the desire that rises above all says 'I will not perish'.
447.nuance: நீர்க்குமிழி, the water bubble, is the Naladiyar's image for the body (27). ஆர்க்கும் உயர் ஆசை may be the desire higher than all others or the desire that rises in everyone; it closes the run of speaking desires.

448.reading: Even seeing, eye to eye before one's own eyes, bodies burn on the log, the thought comes that we will remain firm.
448.nuance: கண்ணுக்குக் கண்ணெதிரே doubles the seeing: the pyre is not hearsay. The verse states the contradiction without explaining it, which is the lament's manner.

449.reading: The thought fondly takes the impermanent for the permanent; it says 'I will not be alone' and 'I will not forget myself'.
449.nuance: அநித்தியத்தை நித்தியமென்று is the Kural's definition of the lowest understanding (331). தனை மறக்கேன் is the self refusing to forget itself, the opposite of the self-forgetting the mystics ask for; ஆதரவாய் (with fondness) marks the error as an attachment, not a mistake.

450.reading: The pit of hell says 'I will still eat you'; the loins like a serpent's hood say 'I will ruin you'.
450.nuance: அல்குல், the woman's loins, compared to the cobra's spread hood (உரகப் படம்), is a stock figure of love poetry turned into a threat; here the body part itself speaks, as the desires did. The hell pit and the loins are set as parallel devourers.

451.reading: The breasts like young coconuts say 'I will ruin your house'; the eyes like buds say 'I will eat your life'.
451.nuance: குரும்பை (the young coconut) and அரும்பு (the bud) are conventional comparisons for breasts and eyes; the lament keeps the conventions and makes them threats. குடி கெடுத்தல் is to ruin a family or lineage.

452.reading: Death, taking a woman's form, plans his deceit; without support here I melt like lac.
452.nuance: மறலி is Yama. அரக்காய் உருகுதல், melting like lac or sealing wax, is the image of helpless dissolving; 450 to 452 together make the woman's body the disguise of death, the view Tirumular prescribes as a meditation at 1953.

453.reading: Lord of Kannivanam who in grace bore Kandan: by what means shall I climb up and spread?
453.nuance: The Lord is identified by fatherhood of Kandan (Murugan), so Siva. ஏறிப் படருதல் (to climb and spread, as a creeper does) is the ascent out of the condition described in 434 to 452; the verse is the first direct plea, and the question is left open.

454.reading: Are the days that dawned as grass and as shrub not enough? Are the days that passed as stone and as tree not enough?
454.nuance: The போதாதோ litany, running to 465, counts births through the orders of beings and asks the Lord whether their sum is not yet sufficient to earn release. புல்லாகிப் பூடாய் echoes the famous ladder of births in Manikkavasagar's Sivapuranam, which begins with the same two words; stones and trees count as births.

455.reading: Are the days ruined as mongoose and as ram not enough? Are the days spent as water creatures and as crawling things not enough?
455.nuance: கிடம் is probably கிடாய், the ram or goat; நீரியாய் (as a water-dweller) and ஊர்வன (reptiles, crawlers) follow the traditional classes of living things (ஊர்வன, பறப்பன, நீந்துவன).

456.reading: Are the days gone as elements and as gods not enough? Are the days fallen as demons who inflict torment not enough?
456.nuance: பூதம் may mean ghosts or goblins rather than the elements; both are classes of birth in the traditional count, and gods (தேவர்) and asuras (தானவர்) are set side by side as equally births to be left.

457.reading: Are the days destroyed in the mother's womb not enough? Are the days lived as a king and died not enough?
457.nuance: Death in the womb and a king's death are put together: the shortest and the grandest human life count the same in the tally.

458.reading: Are the days sunk low as a mother and as a wife not enough? Are the days gone as a child and as a man not enough?
458.nuance: The poet counts female births among his own (தாயாகித் தாரமாய்), so the soul has no sex across lives. தாழ்ந்த (sunk, lowered) is the verb for the women's births, which may be the poet's judgment on those roles or on the dependence they bring.

links.note: Sivavakkiyar says children, wives and kin are maya and none of them can come along when Yama calls; Pattinathar has the desire for children and kin itself refuse to forget him. Both treat the bond of kin as the thing that does not leave.

Pattinathar's five senses say they will not subside and he turns to the Lord; Tirumular says the senses come under control of themselves once one meets the Lord alone. Both place the subduing of the senses with the Lord rather than with effort.

Kakapusundar's dance comes when one is without desire and anger and has forgotten mother and kin; Pattinathar's lust and anger refuse to pass and his kin-desire refuses to forget. The same two items block the same goal from opposite sides.
The body as a bubble on water: the Naladiyar praises those firm enough to see it so and end their wandering; Pattinathar confesses that his thought takes the bubble for permanent.
Tirumular's streaming body goes like a bubble on flowing water into the Supreme; Pattinathar's water-bubble body is what desire wrongly holds as lasting. One image, used for merging and for delusion.

Tirumular's body-tenders end mounted on a pyre of rough logs; Pattinathar sees bodies burn on the log before his eyes and still thinks he will stay. Both make the cremation log the refutation of the body's care.
The Kural calls taking what does not last for lasting the lowest understanding; Pattinathar confesses that very thought in himself, and adds that it is held fondly (ஆதரவாய்).
Tirumular addresses those who feel the unstaying state as lasting and the perishing hut as permanent; Pattinathar is such a one speaking of himself.

Tirumular prescribes thinking of women as Death come to kill so that desire falls away; Pattinathar states it as his experience, Death taking a woman's form to deceive him, while his desire has not fallen away.

Sivavakkiyar: gathered from atoms through every kind of womb you were born human and now lose yourselves in books; Pattinathar counts the same passage through the orders of birth and asks whether it is not yet enough.

Arunagirinathar asks how many bodies, countless as sand, he has filled, in the sea, on hills and in springs; Pattinathar's litany of births as elements, gods and demons is the same count put to the Lord as a plea that it suffice.

source_issues: The refrain கன்னிவனநாதா is printed as a separate line inside every fourth unit (438, 442, 446, 449, 454, 458) rather than as a line of each, so those units have three lines and the rest two.
446 line 2 கைச்சு மின்னுமான் is obscure and may be corrupt.
